narrative:
The review predicted a 56.1% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly above even, not a certainty, but it was high enough for your law school application to be denied.

The strongest reason was your third-year class-standing decile: you were in the first decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. Because this was the most influential factor, it pushed the prediction most strongly toward bar-exam failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 was the second most important factor, and it worked in your favor: it is above the accepted-student average of 3.23 and pushed toward passing. The third most important factor was your first-year class-standing decile. You were again in the first decile, compared with an accepted average near the sixth decile, and this pushed toward failure. Thus, your GPA was a positive signal, but it was outweighed by the very low first- and third-year standing measures, especially the third-year standing.

To improve a future application, focus on demonstrating stronger academic performance in advanced law coursework and ask admissions for feedback on how to address the class-standing concern. Consider retaking the LSAT, since your 29.50 is below the accepted average of 37.18, and apply to programs where your record can be reviewed holistically after you have added stronger evidence of readiness for bar study.
